title: In 96 held-out OpenNeuro studies of mostly task fMRI, whole thalamus, brainstem and ventral diencephalon signals peaked with or after the cortical global signal in cross-correlation, not before it
abstract:
In fMRI from many public studies, the signals of the whole thalamus, brainstem and ventral diencephalon (hypothalamus and nearby nuclei) peaked in cross-correlation at the same time as the brain-wide cortical signal or slightly after it, not before it. This matters because earlier studies proposed that these arousal-related regions lead the brain-wide (global) fMRI signal by 1-6 s, which would make them a simple arousal marker.

We used ReadyNeuro: minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro BOLD fMRI at 1 s per frame, without slice-timing correction. Regions came from each subject's segmentation. The reference was the mean cortical grey-matter signal (global signal, GS). We fixed the discovery studies before we read data, found the pattern in 17 studies, and pre-registered 15 tests. All passed in 68 held-out studies (Holm p <= 0.0033) and in all 96 held-out studies; a later stage of 28 studies passed 12 of 15 with the same signs but missed the pass criterion for the thalamus. Most runs (88 %) were task runs.

Pooled cross-correlation peak lags, corrected for slice timing (positive = later than cortex): thalamus +0.08 s, brainstem +0.21 s, ventral diencephalon +0.08 s, an approximate basal forebrain region -0.08 s. The putamen led by 0.49 s (positive control; not shown in rest-only runs). Post hoc phase analysis: at 0.01-0.03 Hz the thalamus, brainstem and ventral diencephalon were 6-18 degrees later; at 0.06-0.1 Hz their phase was not different from 0. The phase slope ("group delay") was negative (-0.3 to -0.9 s), so the timing is not one delay, and we do not claim a lag or lead in seconds.

Global-signal regression (GSR) compressed the lags and made the brainstem early (+0.26 to -0.11 s). The thalamic dip 4-8 s before global peaks, earlier read as an arousal lead, was present but smaller than the cerebellar dip. After ventricle regression the broadband lags stayed at or above 0, but the 0.06-0.1 Hz phase of the ventral diencephalon became early. A slice-timing model recovered known delays in sequential acquisitions (slope 1.03); results without correction were the same.

State effects were weak: the pre-registered rest-minus-task thalamic measure was +0.71 s (p = 0.08, 28 studies), and a pre-registered sleep test (EEG-scored, 7-11 subjects) did not pass.

Limits: small nuclei (locus coeruleus, raphe, nucleus basalis) are not resolved, the basal forebrain region is approximate, there is no physiology in the main sets, and vascular timing was not measured.

No region led the cortex in any stage; the pre-registered N2-minus-wake test did not pass.
